newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan won't yield dignity to witness HK handover.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan won't yield dignity to witness HK handover.

text.p: Taiwan said on Wednesday its officials would not witness a gala ceremony marking Hong Kong's handover to Beijing if attendance came at the expense of the estranged island's dignity.

Kao Koong-lian, vice chairman of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, said whoever Hong Kong or Beijing invites to represent Taiwan at the June 30 ceremony could accept only if accorded proper respect.
Kao made clear this meant treating Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as something other than a mere province of the communist People's Republic of China.
"It is simply unacceptable if the (Taiwan) representatives are seated with the mainland's provincial representatives," Kao told a news conference.

Beijing has viewed Taiwan as a rebel-held province since a civil war split them in 1949, pressing ever harder to force the island's exiled Republic of China government out of existence so Taiwan can be reabsorbed under mainland sovereignty.
Taipei maintains that its Chinese Nationalist republic has status equal to that of China's national government.
Kao said it was not up to Taipei to say who would attend the midnight handover gala, indicating that Hong Kong or Beijing should take the initiative.
"It is not for the government to decide who we will send for the handover ceremony," Kao said. "We don't know who will be invited to attend the ceremony at this moment."
Whoever does go will share the historic limelight with the Taiwan government's key adversaries -- Chinese President and Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng.
Beijing affirmed on Wednesday that Jiang and Li would attend.
Beijing says the long-negotiated return of Hong Kong and Portuguese-ruled Macau in 1999 will leave Taiwan as the only territory still awaiting "reunification with the motherland".
China says its handling of Hong Kong's return under a "one country, two systems" model of political and economic autonomy of should reassure Taiwan of its own future with the mainland.
Under the system agreed by Britain and China in 1984, Hong Kong can maintain its capitalist system for 50 years.

Since the 1949 split, Taipei has officially favoured eventual reunification with the mainland, but flatly rejects the "one country, two systems" model, arguing that Beijing has never fully dislodged the exiled republic's sovereignty.
"We have been a sovereign political entity, while Hong Kong has been a colony," Lin Chong-pin, another Mainland Affairs Council vice chairman, told Reuters on Wednesday.
"Therefore Hong Kong is categorically different from the situation we are in and this 'one country, two systems' formula cannot be applied to us," Lin said.
Taiwan, which has embraced multiparty democracy, maintains that reunification is impossible before the Communist Party drops its power monopoly and allows political liberalisation.
"We are a democracy. The government cannot go against the will of the people," Lin said.

Hong Kong's handover does pose new challenges to Taiwan, which relies on the territory as the main point of transit for some US$30 billion in Taiwanese "unofficial" investment that has flowed into the mainland since a late 1980s political thaw.
Kao said Taipei soon would issue a major policy paper laying out the government's views on Hong Kong's changing status and the future of ties between Taiwan, Hong Kong and the mainland.
He declined to give details.
